finding.claim: list_users_sorted concatenates the raw $_GET['sort'] value into an ORDER BY clause and runs it with PDO::query, giving SQL injection in the ORDER BY position. An attacker can read arbitrary data from any table (including sqlite_master) by boolean-style inference from row ordering.
finding.source: list.php:5 - $_GET['sort'] (HTTP query string, fully attacker-controlled; defaults to 'id' only when the parameter is absent)
finding.sink: list.php:6 - $pdo->query("SELECT id, name FROM users ORDER BY " . $sort) run against sqlite app.db

trace.note: string concatenation into SQL text; no quoting, no allowlist, no prepared statement
PDO::query executes the composed SQL; SQLite accepts arbitrary expressions, including scalar subqueries and CASE, in ORDER BY

finding.guards_checked: Only the '?? id' default, which handles absence, not content. No allowlist (ORDER BY cannot be parameterized, so an allowlist is required), no type or regex check on $sort. Stacked queries are not possible because PDO::query runs one statement, so impact is read-only expressions, not writes. PRECONDITION: no caller of list_users_sorted exists in this tree (list.php never invokes any function), so exploitability depends on an entry point not shown here that passes request input to this function. Confirm reachability before treating as live.

verdict.guard_found: none. list.php:5 takes $_GET['sort'] ?? 'id' with no allowlist, regex, or type check, and list.php:6 concatenates it straight into the ORDER BY string passed to $pdo->query(). The safe variant at list.php:11-12 is a separate function and is not called by list_users_sorted.
verdict.reason: The trace is accurate (list.php:5 takes $_GET['sort'] unfiltered and list.php:6 concatenates it into a PDO::query), and no guard sits between input and sink. But the only file in the tree (list.php) defines list_users_sorted at line 4 and never calls it, so no attacker-reachable entry point is visible, and the finding is exploitable only if an unseen caller passes request input to it.
